JPMorgan Chase discloses that its regulatory capital framework is set by the Federal Reserve for the Firm as a consolidated financial holding company, and by the OCC for its principal insured depository institution (IDI) subsidiary, JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. [JPM_2026-08-06_0e5c9f2e00]. Under Basel III, the Firm must maintain minimum ratios for CET1 capital, Tier 1 capital, Total capital, Tier 1 leverage, and the SLR; failure to meet these could cause the Federal Reserve to take action [JPM_2026-08-06_0e5c9f2e00][JPM_2026-02-13_3b45b9ac7b]. Basel III prescribes two approaches for calculating risk-weighted assets—Standardized and Advanced—and capital adequacy is evaluated against the lower of the two versus the applicable requirements [JPM_2026-02-13_3b45b9ac7b].

For the BHC, the risk-based requirements (as of June 30, 2026 and December 31, 2025) were CET1 of 11.5%, Tier 1 of 13.0%, and Total capital of 15.0% under both the Standardized and Advanced approaches; for JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. the corresponding requirements were 7.0%, 8.5%, and 10.5% [JPM_2026-08-06_0e5c9f2e00]. The Firm's requirements embed a minimum plus a 4.5% GSIB surcharge (Method 2) and either a 2.5% stress capital buffer (Standardized) or a fixed 2.5% capital conservation buffer (Advanced), with the countercyclical buffer currently at 0%; the IDI includes a fixed 2.5% capital conservation buffer and is not subject to the GSIB surcharge [JPM_2026-08-06_0e5c9f2e00]. For the year ended December 31, 2024, the Firm's Standardized requirements were higher, at 12.3% (CET1), 13.8% (Tier 1), and 15.8% (Total capital), versus 11.5%, 13.0%, and 15.0% under Advanced [JPM_2026-02-13_3b45b9ac7b].

On leverage-based measures (as of June 30, 2026), the Tier 1 leverage requirement is 4.0% for both BHC and IDI, and the SLR requirement is 4.3% for the BHC and 4.0% for the IDI [JPM_2026-08-06_0e5c9f2e00]. These reflect the eSLR final rule, which the Firm early-adopted effective January 1, 2026; for the year ended December 31, 2025, the SLR requirements were higher at 5.0% (BHC) and 6.0% (IDI), comprised of a 3.0% minimum SLR plus supplementary leverage buffers of 2.0% and 3.0%, respectively [JPM_2026-05-01_9ab083b20e].

The filings also disclose actual compliance: as of March 31, 2026, JPMorgan Chase & Co. and JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. were well-capitalized and met all capital requirements, with the Firm reporting a Standardized CET1 ratio of 14.3%, Tier 1 of 15.2%, and Total capital of 17.2% [JPM_2026-05-01_9ab083b20e]. Similarly, as of December 31, 2025 and 2024, both entities were well-capitalized and met all applicable requirements [JPM_2026-02-13_7b49aa7df1]. Additionally, the Firm disclosed the full phase-out of the $2.9 billion CECL capital transition benefit (which had left a $720 million CET1 benefit at December 31, 2024) as of January 1, 2025, and noted that JPMorgan Chase Bank, N.A. could pay approximately $30.1 billion in dividends to the Parent without prior regulatory approval at January 1, 2026 [JPM_2026-02-13_7b49aa7df1][JPM_2026-02-13_3b45b9ac7b].

**Pfizer's patent-expiration risk disclosures**

Pfizer's principal risk-factor disclosure centers on the loss, expiration, or invalidation of intellectual property rights, along with patent-litigation settlements/judgments and the expiration of co-promotion and licensing rights, which it states can have a material adverse effect on revenues [PFE_2026-02-26_7dede4af36][PFE_2026-02-26_33feda3266].

The company explains the mechanics of the risk: once patent protection expires — or is lost early through a successful legal challenge — Pfizer typically loses market exclusivity on the affected products, and generic and biosimilar manufacturers generally produce identical or highly similar products sold at a lower price [PFE_2026-02-26_33feda3266]. Importantly, the date generic or biosimilar competition commences may differ from the patent or regulatory-exclusivity expiration date, but once competition begins, the resulting price competition can substantially decrease revenues, often within a very short period of time [PFE_2026-02-26_33feda3266]. Similarly, if a product-related patent is found invalid in judicial, court, regulatory, or administrative proceedings, generics or biosimilars could be introduced, eroding sales of existing products; Pfizer also flags exposure to claims that its own IP infringes third-party patents [PFE_2026-02-26_33feda3266].

Pfizer quantifies the exposure: certain products have already experienced patent-based expirations or loss of regulatory exclusivity in certain markets in recent years, and it expects certain products to face new or increased generic competition over the next few years [PFE_2026-02-26_7dede4af36][PFE_2026-02-26_33feda3266]. It anticipates a significant reduction in revenue from patent-based or regulatory-exclusivity expiries in 2026 through 2030, with the rate of revenue reduction expected to accelerate significantly over the next few years; in 2026 alone, the expected impact is $1.5 billion [PFE_2026-02-26_7dede4af36]. Pfizer also cautions there is no assurance that any particular product will maintain market exclusivity for the full period reflected in its Form 10-K estimates or assumed in its financial guidance [PFE_2026-02-26_33feda3266].

The company states it continues to vigorously defend its patent rights against infringement and supports efforts to strengthen worldwide recognition of patent rights [PFE_2026-02-26_7dede4af36][PFE_2026-02-26_33feda3266].

Finally, the filing's patent-footnote detail illustrates product-specific expiration exposure: the apixaban basic patent and associated SPC were invalidated in the U.K. with additional challenges pending elsewhere [PFE_2026-02-26_b6e1f07146]; Xtandi received interim patent-term extensions to December 2026 with applications pending to 2028 [PFE_2026-02-26_b6e1f07146]; Vyndaqel's basic patent expiry in Japan is August 2026, with Vynmac's cardiomyopathy regulatory exclusivity expiring in March 2029 [PFE_2026-02-26_b6e1f07146]; Xalkori SPCs have been extended to 2028 in France, Germany, and Italy [PFE_2026-02-26_b6e1f07146]; and Mektovi's U.S. expiry has interim extensions from March 2026 to March 2027, with an application to extend to August 2027 [PFE_2026-02-26_b6e1f07146].

NVIDIA's filings describe a business that has been subject to a "series of shifting and expanding export control restrictions" that impact its ability to serve customers outside the United States [NVDA_2026-05-20_9c3fedce35]. The filings note that U.S. and allied stakeholders increasingly focus export controls on AI-associated semiconductors, including GPUs, and that the U.S. has already imposed unilateral worldwide controls restricting GPUs; additional unilateral or multilateral controls are considered likely [NVDA_2025-11-19_6c3a6f3e35].

**Timeline of restrictions.** The filings trace the history of U.S. government (USG) actions: in August 2022 the USG announced export restrictions and licensing requirements targeting China's semiconductor and supercomputing industries, which impacted certain chips as well as software, hardware, equipment and technology used to develop and manufacture certain chips to China (including Hong Kong and Macau) and Russia, and specifically impacted NVIDIA's A100 and H100 integrated circuits and systems incorporating them [NVDA_2026-05-20_9c3fedce35]. In July 2023, the USG added a licensing requirement for a subset of A100 and H100 products destined to certain customers and regions, including some countries in the Middle East [NVDA_2026-05-20_9c3fedce35]. In October 2023, the USG announced new and updated licensing requirements for exports to China and Country Groups D:1, D:4 and D:5 (including Saudi Arabia, the UAE, and Vietnam, but excluding Israel) for products exceeding certain performance thresholds, including the A100, A800, H100, H800, L4, L40, L40S RTX 4090, GB200 NVL72 and B200 [NVDA_2026-05-20_9c3fedce35].

**Business impacts.** The filings state these controls "have been and may again be very broad in scope and application," potentially prohibiting NVIDIA from exporting to any or all customers in one or more markets, negatively affecting its manufacturing, testing and warehousing locations, and limiting its ability to serve demand abroad [NVDA_2025-11-19_6c3a6f3e35]. Export controls have negatively impacted demand not only in China but also in other markets such as Europe, Latin America and Southeast Asia [NVDA_2025-11-19_1b25f32a98][NVDA_2026-02-25_714efcc8b8][NVDA_2026-05-20_5fd1603edb]. They have disrupted (and could again disrupt) supply chains and distribution channels, including for non-data-center products [NVDA_2025-11-19_6c3a6f3e35], and have created compliance burdens on NVIDIA, its customers, partners and suppliers [NVDA_2025-11-19_6c3a6f3e35][NVDA_2026-02-25_714efcc8b8].

**Competitive and demand effects.** The filings warn export controls have a "disproportionate impact on NVIDIA" relative to competitors selling chips outside the scope of the controls, have encouraged customers to "design-out" certain U.S. semiconductors, and have encouraged overseas governments to push customers to buy from competitors rather than NVIDIA [NVDA_2025-11-19_1b25f32a98][NVDA_2026-02-25_714efcc8b8][NVDA_2026-05-20_5fd1603edb]. Controls also increase investment risk in advanced products because a new product may become subject to new controls by the time it reaches market, resulting in excess inventory and purchase obligations "as we recently experienced with the H20" [NVDA_2025-11-19_1b25f32a98][NVDA_2026-02-25_714efcc8b8][NVDA_2026-05-20_5fd1603edb].

The USG has imposed license conditions limiting foreign firms' ability to offer large-scale GPU clusters and may require chip tracking and throttling mechanisms; such mandates could introduce system vulnerabilities and liabilities [NVDA_2025-11-19_1b25f32a98][NVDA_2026-05-20_5fd1603edb]. The USG has already restricted certain gaming GPUs, and export controls may disrupt NVIDIA's supply/distribution chain for products warehoused in and distributed from Hong Kong [NVDA_2025-11-19_1b25f32a98][NVDA_2026-05-20_5fd1603edb]. Controls on data center GPUs may also reduce demand for NVIDIA networking products, and the USG may extend controls to networking products such as high-speed interconnects to limit downstream large-cluster training [NVDA_2025-11-19_1b25f32a98][NVDA_2026-02-25_714efcc8b8][NVDA_2026-05-20_5fd1603edb]. Even non-binding draft legislation has had effects: after U.S. legislative proposals calling for mandatory chip features, China's government publicly questioned whether H20 products had built-in vulnerabilities, discouraging purchases (NVIDIA says its GPUs do not include such vulnerabilities) [NVDA_2025-11-19_1b25f32a98][NVDA_2026-05-20_5fd1603edb].

**Foreign-government responses and China-specific issues.** The filings note export restrictions may provoke responses from foreign governments, including China, that negatively affect NVIDIA's supply chain or its ability to serve customers worldwide, which could substantially reduce revenue [NVDA_2025-11-19_6c3a6f3e35]. On September 15, 2025, China's antitrust regulators preliminarily found that NVIDIA's compliance with U.S. export controls — which required offering degraded products to the Chinese market — discriminated against Chinese customers and violated the terms of China's approval of the Mellanox acquisition; adverse conclusions could expose NVIDIA to financial penalties, restrictions on its business, or orders regarding its networking business in China [NVDA_2025-11-19_6c3a6f3e35][NVDA_2026-05-20_9c3fedce35]. Additionally, the Chinese government has encouraged customers to buy from China-based competitors and discouraged use of NVIDIA data center products, and a Chinese Action Plan endorsing new compute-efficiency standards could further restrict use of NVIDIA data center products if the company ever regained market access [NVDA_2026-02-25_714efcc8b8].

['You should carefully consider the following risks and uncertainties, together with all other information in this Annual Report on Form 10-K. Any of the risk factors we describe below could adversely affect our business, financial condition or results of operations and the market price of our common stock.
Risks related to commercialization and our products
Regulatory and market uncertainty have and may continue to impact our business and the markets for our products.
Our ability to successfully commercialize our approved vaccines and any future products depends in part on evolving regulatory requirements, public health recommendations and market acceptance. In 2025, changes at U.S. regulatory agencies impacted policies and priorities related to our industry. For example, changes in FDA regulatory policies, post-marketing safety monitoring, and evidentiary expectations, as well as CDC and Advisory Committee on Immunization Practices (ACIP) recommendations regarding eligibility, target populations, and vaccination practices, may have affected and may continue to affect demand for our vaccines. Some of these changes, including new post-marketing commitments, have impacted and may in the future impact our costs. Ongoing regulatory uncertainty and evolving regulatory and public health guidance could impact future approvals, advisory committee recommendations, acceptance and demand for our existing or future products.
Vaccination rates in the future may also be lower than our expectations due to other factors, including viral evolution, medical need and consumer motivation to vaccinate. These and other factors may make it difficult to accurately forecast vaccination rates for our products. If demand for COVID vaccines continues to decline, we lose significant market share, or our products are subject to significant competitive pricing pressure, our product sales may not materialize consistent with our projections. Beyond COVID, we have experienced challenges in the RSV market, in part due to advisory committee recommendations that were more limited than anticipated.
Furthermore, our decisions regarding seasonal vaccine development, including for COVID-19, will be informed by annual guidance from the FDA and foreign regulators, which may impact the timing of development for our COVID vaccines. Different regulators have in the past and may in the future issue varying guidance regarding vaccine composition or populations who should receive a vaccine. Additionally, if our efforts to develop variant-specific vaccines are delayed or not as successful as our competitors', we could suffer reputational harm, loss of market share and adverse financial results. We may expend significant resources adapting our vaccines or conducting clinical trials to protect against variants, but a market for our adapted vaccines may fail to develop or demand may not align with our projections or cost expenditures.
We may experience difficulties executing our near-term strategy and prioritized pipeline.
While we expect to launch multiple new products over the next several years, our ability to commercialize our pipeline is subject to many risks, including those described elsewhere in these Risk Factors under "Risks related to our pipeline, product development and regulatory review" and "Risks related to the manufacturing of our commercial products and product candidates." If we do not successfully execute our near-term plan for growing our infectious disease vaccine franchise, our ability to invest in our pipeline, including our oncology and rare disease programs, may suffer.
Furthermore, our broad clinical success and post-pandemic commercial challenges have necessitated a more selective and paced approach to our research and development investment. If we do not successfully implement our cost efficiency and prioritization programs, we may fail to meet our cash breakeven goal. Additionally, as we pursue development of our prioritized programs, we may forego or delay pursuit of other opportunities that could prove to have greater commercial potential. If our prioritized programs are unsuccessful, or not as successful as others could have been, we may be unable to realize a sustainable return on our investments and or achieve long-term growth.
The vaccine market, and pharmaceutical market more generally, is intensely competitive, and we may be unable to compete effectively in the market for existing or new products, treatment methods or technologies.
We compete with larger, well-established and experienced pharmaceutical companies for sales of our products, including against Pfizer and San', "Moderna is a pioneer and leader in the field of mRNA medicine. Through the advancement of our technology platform, we are reimagining how medicines are made to transform how we treat and prevent diseases. Since our founding, our mRNA platform has enabled the development of vaccine and therapeutic candidates across infectious disease, oncology, rare disease and more.
With a global team and a unique culture, driven by our values and mindsets, our mission is to deliver the greatest possible impact to people through mRNA medicines.
We currently have three commercial products-Spikevax and mNEXSPIKE (our COVID vaccines) and mRESVIA (our vaccine against respiratory syncytial virus (RSV)). mNEXSPIKE, which we launched commercially in the third quarter of 2025, is now our leading product in the U.S. retail channel. In 2025, we achieved total revenue of $1.9 billion, largely from sales of our COVID vaccines.
Beyond our commercial products, we continue to demonstrate the potential of our platform technology and are advancing a pipeline of development candidates across oncology, rare disease and infectious disease. In January 2026, we and Merck announced five-year data from the Phase 2b study of intismeran autogene (mRNA-4157), our mRNA-based individualized neoantigen therapy, in combination with Merck's pembrolizumab (KEYTRUDA®), which demonstrated sustained improvement in recurrence-free survival in patients with high-risk melanoma (stage III/IV) following complete resection. We are advancing intismeran in collaboration with Merck, with eight Phase 2 and Phase 3 clinical trials underway across multiple tumor types. **Reliance on COVID-19 vaccine revenue.** The filing shows COVID vaccines are the dominant revenue driver: Moderna reports three commercial products—Spikevax and mNEXSPIKE (COVID vaccines) and mRESVIA (RSV)—and states that 2025 total revenue of $1.9 billion came "largely from sales of our COVID vaccines" [MRNA_2026-02-20_b9a7ddf56d]. On the demand side, Moderna warns that regulatory and public health dynamics—FDA policy changes, post-marketing safety monitoring, and CDC/ACIP recommendations on eligibility and target populations—may continue to depress vaccine demand and raise costs [MRNA_2026-02-20_b6770f650a]. ## Comparison: J&J vs. BMS Litigation Risk Disclosures

### Johnson & Johnson
Johnson & Johnson's Item 1A risk factors explicitly disclose that the Company is "subject to significant legal proceedings" spanning product liability, patent disputes, and claims that its sales, marketing and pricing practices violate antitrust, unfair trade practices and/or consumer protection laws [JNJ_2026-02-11_0af6ebef58]. It states its more significant proceedings are detailed in Note 19 "Legal proceedings" to the consolidated financial statements [JNJ_2026-02-11_0af6ebef58]. The most prominent matter identified is the "numerous lawsuits" arising out of body powders containing talc, primarily JOHNSON'S Baby Powder, where the company is a defendant and faces potentially material settlements or judgments, including joint and several liability [JNJ_2026-02-11_0af6ebef58]. The filing also discloses that litigation can involve thousands of plaintiffs, large and/or indeterminate damage amounts including punitive or exemplary damages, and that resolution of these matters "could have a material adverse effect on the Company's results of operations and cash flows" [JNJ_2026-02-11_0af6ebef58]. Notably, J&J carries no third-party product liability insurance, relying instead on a wholly owned captive insurance company subject to certain limits [JNJ_2026-02-11_0af6ebef58]. Additional risk-factor detail covers product-recall litigation, FDA regulatory action, false-claims investigations and potential debarment from government healthcare programs [JNJ_2026-02-11_0af6ebef58].

### Bristol-Myers Squibb
The retrieved context from BMS's own filings does not contain the substance of its litigation disclosure. The BMS 10-K chunk shows only the "Item 3. Legal Proceedings" heading in the table of contents; the body text describing any ongoing proceedings was not captured in the retrieved excerpts [BMY_2026-02-11_4d235195f6]. The other BMS chunks cover only the definitions of abbreviated terms, the exhibit index and executive certifications [BMY_2026-07-30_e9e867e0b3][BMY_2026-02-11_e53377dd95]. The only litigation reference involving BMS in the retrieved context appears in Pfizer's 10-K, which reports that BMS and Pfizer jointly filed a patent infringement action in the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware in December 2025 against Azurity Pharmaceuticals over a proposed generic apixaban (Eliquis) product [PFE_2026-02-26_512af3d873]. That disclosure, however, comes from Pfizer's filing, not from BMS's own risk disclosure, and it describes BMS as a co-plaintiff in a patent matter rather than a named defendant in significant adverse proceedings.

### Conclusion
Based on the retrieved filings, Johnson & Johnson's own filing discloses materially more significant ongoing legal proceedings — most notably the talc/body-powder litigation, together with product-liability, patent, antitrust and regulatory-exposure risk factors — than what is visible for Bristol-Myers Squibb [JNJ_2026-02-11_0af6ebef58]. However, I don't have enough information in the retrieved filings to describe what BMS itself discloses about its own legal proceedings, because the substantive text of its Item 3 Legal Proceedings disclosure was not included in the retrieved context [BMY_2026-02-11_4d235195f6]. ## Competition Risk Factors: AMD vs. Intel

### AMD

AMD frames competition primarily as a **pricing and market-power threat from two dominant incumbents**. It notes that competitors may have stronger market positions, larger customer bases, more design wins, and greater financial/sales/marketing/distribution resources, allowing them to acquire share and capitalize on new opportunities more efficiently [AMD_2026-05-06_978a5892ae]. It specifically calls out Intel, which "uses its microprocessor market position to price its products aggressively and target our customers and channel partners with special incentives," reducing AMD's unit sales and average selling prices [AMD_2026-05-06_978a5892ae]. It separately flags Nvidia, which "leverages its market position in data center GPU, financial resources, and proprietary software ecosystem" to promote its systems and influence customers [AMD_2026-05-06_978a5892ae].

AMD also emphasizes **new structural competitive threats**: competitors pursuing alternative architectures such as Arm could grow the Arm ecosystem and reduce demand in consumer, commercial, and data center markets [AMD_2026-05-06_978a5892ae]; and it faces competition from customers that internally develop products to support AI workloads similar to AMD's [AMD_2026-05-06_978a5892ae]. Finally, AMD highlights **competitor consolidation** — specifically the September 2025 Nvidia partnership and investment in Intel — as a source of increased competition and pricing pressure [AMD_2026-05-06_978a5892ae].

### Intel

Intel's competition discussion is more **strategic and self-reflective**, centered on its own repositioning and lost ground rather than on named rivals' tactics. Intel acknowledges it "has lost market share in recent years, including in both client and data center markets," in x86 products and more broadly, and that its data center business was negatively impacted by the shift of customer spend toward AI-optimized GPUs, "a rapidly developing and very significant compute market where we have been unsuccessful to date in becoming a meaningful participant" [INTC_2026-01-23_468e1987a1].

Intel emphasizes **the ecosystem/custom-silicon threat from customers and new architectures**: internally developed semiconductors from OEMs and cloud service providers (who vertically integrate designs with software assets), ARM-based products and ecosystem growth, and hyperscalers moving to custom or semi-custom products [INTC_2026-01-23_3842f5432d]. It names competitors across its portfolio — platform products (AMD, Qualcomm), GPUs (NVIDIA, AMD), ASICs, memory, storage, connectivity/networking, and other semiconductors — and notes many competitors have substantially greater financial resources [INTC_2026-01-23_3842f5432d].

Uniquely, Intel emphasizes **its manufacturing position as both a liability and a new front of competition**. As an integrated device manufacturer, Intel carries higher capex and R&D than fabless competitors whose foundry partners (TSMC, Samsung) keep improving their offerings [INTC_2026-01-23_468e1987a1]. It also flags its limited experience in the third-party foundry business, facing intense competition from TSMC, Samsung, GlobalFoundries, UMC, and SMIC, with the DCAI segment naming AMD (x86 CPUs/GPUs/accelerators), Nvidia GPU systems, hyperscaler custom silicon, ARM/RISC-V entrants, and Broadcom in custom ASICs [INTC_2026-01-23_468e1987a1][INTC_2026-01-23_14a54b0498]. Intel additionally highlights **geopolitical/new-entrant risk**, including China's programs to promote a domestic semiconductor industry and supply chains [INTC_2026-01-23_468e1987a1].

### Comparison conclusion

AMD emphasizes being **squeezed between two well-resourced incumbents** (Intel's pricing aggression and Nvidia's ecosystem lock-in), competitor partnerships/consolidation, and architecture/customer-driven substitution as threats to its unit sales and margins [AMD_2026-05-06_978a5892ae]. Intel's framing is more **strategic and introspective**: its risks center on lost market share, being a late/no participant in AI GPUs, the rise of custom silicon and ARM, and — unique to Intel — its IDM/foundry strategy, where higher capex, TSMC/Samsung's foundry improvements, foundry competition, and new Chinese entrants all bear directly on its competitive position [INTC_2026-01-23_468e1987a1][INTC_2026-01-23_3842f5432d][INTC_2026-01-23_14a54b0498].

## Pfizer vs. Gilead: Loss-of-Exclusivity Risk

### Gilead Sciences
Gilead's 10-K discloses a patent-expiration table for its principal products [GILD_2026-02-24_97637b20a7]. The earliest expirations are **Livdelzi (2025)**, **Tecartus (2027)**, and **Trodelvy (2028)**; for Tecartus the composition-of-matter patent has already expired in the EU [GILD_2026-02-24_97637b20a7]. After that, the next cluster is Genvoya (2029 U.S.), though the cobicistat-related patent license does not begin until August 6, 2032 under the Apotex/MSN settlement [GILD_2026-02-24_97637b20a7]. Gilead's core revenue base is protected well into the 2030s: Descovy and Vemlidy (2031), Odefsey (2032), Epclusa (2033 U.S./2032 EU), and Biktarvy (2036, with no generic entry expected prior to April 1, 2036), Veklury (2036), Sunlenca and Yeztugo/Yeytuo (2037) [GILD_2026-02-24_97637b20a7]. U.S. regulatory exclusivity for one referenced product expires in 2032 [GILD_2026-02-24_97637b20a7]. The disclosed context does not quantify a near-term revenue dollar impact from these expirations.

### Pfizer
Pfizer's 10-K provides a basic product patent expiration table with **multiple near-term expirations**: Xeljanz (2026), Prevnar 13/Prevenar 13 (2026), Eliquis (2027 U.S./2026 EU), Ibrance (2027), Xtandi (2027), Vyndaqel/Vyndamax (2026), and Xalkori (2027) [PFE_2026-02-26_3de595f7e1]. Pfizer explicitly states it anticipates "a significant reduction of revenue from patent-based or regulatory exclusivity expiries in 2026 through 2030," with the rate of revenue decline accelerating [PFE_2026-02-26_33feda3266][PFE_2026-02-26_7dede4af36]. It quantifies the near-term impact: ~**$1.5 billion** in 2026 in the 10-K [PFE_2026-02-26_7dede4af36], subsequently revised to approximately **$1.1 billion** in the 2026 10-Q [PFE_2026-08-04_23c3cb6560]. The 10-Q further notes IRA Maximum Fair Prices became effective for Eliquis on January 1, 2026, with negotiated prices for Ibrance and Xtandi effective in 2027 [PFE_2026-08-04_23c3cb6560].

### Conclusion
**Pfizer discloses a more near-term loss-of-exclusivity risk.** Multiple significant in-line products (Xeljanz, Prevnar 13, Eliquis, Ibrance, Xtandi, Vyndaqel, Xalkori) expire in 2026–2027, and Pfizer quantifies a ~$1.1–1.5 billion revenue impact in 2026 alone [PFE_2026-02-26_3de595f7e1][PFE_2026-02-26_7dede4af36][PFE_2026-08-04_23c3cb6560]. By contrast, Gilead's near-term exposure (through ~2028) is limited to Livdelzi, Tecartus, Trodelvy, and Genvoya, while its principal products (Descovy, Vemlidy, Odefsey, Epclusa, Biktarvy, Veklury) are protected into the 2031–2037 range [GILD_2026-02-24_97637b20a7].

Market risk is the potential for changes in earnings or the value of financial instruments held by Schwab as a result of fluctuations in interest rates, equity prices, or market conditions. AbbVie's loss-of-exclusivity (LOE) risk is explicitly framed as a top-tier business risk. The company states that patents covering its products normally provide market exclusivity, and that as patents expire it could face competition from lower-priced generics or biosimilars, which "typically is followed promptly by substitutes that may significantly reduce sales for that product in a short amount of time" [ABBV_2026-02-20_155a5aa201]. mRNA transfers the information stored in our genes to the cellular machinery that makes all the proteins required for life. Our genes are stored as sequences of DNA which contain the instructions to make specific proteins. Each mRNA molecule contains the instructions to produce a specific protein with a distinct function in the body. mRNA transmits those instructions to cellular machinery, called ribosomes, that make copies of the required protein.
We see mRNA functioning as the "software of life." mRNA is a linear polymer comprising four monomers called nucleotides: adenosine (A), guanosine (G), cytosine (C) and uridine (U). Within the region of the molecule that codes for a protein (the coding region), the sequence of these four nucleotides forms a language made up of three-letter words called codons. The first codon, or start codon (AUG), signals where the ribosome should start protein synthesis. To know what protein to make, the ribosome then progresses along the mRNA one codon at a time, appending the appropriate amino acid to the growing protein. To end protein synthesis, three different codons (UAA, UAG, and UGA) serve as stop signals, telling the ribosome where to terminate protein synthesis. In total, there are 64 potential codons, but only 20 amino acids that are used to build proteins; therefore, multiple codons can encode for the same amino acid.
